title: Chime banks on resilient consumer spending to post maiden quarterly bottom line
content:
By Pritam Biswas and Arasu Kannagi Basil

May 6 (Reuters) - Chime posted its first-ever quarterly profit on Wednesday, as resilient consumer spending in the first three months ‌of the year lifted demand for the financial technology firm's digital banking products.

Consumer ‌spending remained resilient in the first quarter as individuals and businesses maintained spending trends and supported the payments sector, ​despite broader macroeconomic volatility linked to the war in the Middle East.

Payments processing company Visa also reported a rise in quarterly profit last week, helped by the spending trends. However, analysts and boardrooms have said that they are keeping a keen eye on the proceedings in the ‌Middle East.

"We see broad resilience ⁠and consistency in consumer trends," Finance Chief Matthew Newcomb said in an interview with Reuters.

He added that the company saw growth across both discretionary ⁠and non-discretionary categories.

The company had previously said that it expects to achieve profitability in 2026. New-age fintech offering digital-first services, user-friendly platforms and lower fees have reshaped the banking industry, ramping up competition ​for ​traditional lenders.

Chime's purchase volume, including outbound instant transfer, ​increased 12% year-over-year to $39 billion in ‌the quarter, while active members grew 19% to 10.2 million.

The San Francisco-based company expects second quarter revenue between $633 million and $643 million, compared to Wall Street's expectations of $641 million, according to estimates compiled by LSEG.

The digital bank went public in New York in June 2025 in a strong investor debut, but shares are now trading at just over $21, below the IPO price ‌of $27. Shares are down a little over 13% so ​far in 2026, underperforming the broader markets.

Chime's banking model ​targets everyday Americans, offering several products ​for customers with limited credit histories who rely more on debit than ‌credit, but is expanding to a broader ​product set in 2026 ​including membership tiers and investing.

The company reported a revenue of $647 million, up 25% over last year, in the first quarter that beat the Street's estimates. The company reported ​a net income of $53 ‌million and a net margin of 8%.

The board of directors of the company also ​approved an additional $200 million share repurchase plan.

(Reporting by Pritam Biswas and Arasu ​Kannagi Basil in Bengaluru; Editing by Tasim Zahid)

title: Global Payments Q1 Earnings Beat Estimates on Worldpay Momentum
content:
Global Payments, Inc. GPN reported first-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $2.96, which beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $2.82. The bottom line rose 10% year over year.

Adjusted net revenues improved 29.5% year over year to $2.9 billion. The top line beat the consensus mark by 1.3%.

The strong quarterly earnings benefited from early momentum from the company’s streamlined commerce focus and continued uptake of its Genius platform, including an approximately 90% year-over-year increase in bookings. However, the positives were partly offset by elevated operating expenses.

Global Payments Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS SurpriseGlobal Payments Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Global Payments Inc. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Global Payments Inc. Quote

GPN’s Operating Performance

The Worldpay acquisition and the sale of Issuer Solutions both closed on Jan. 9, 2026, reshaping Global Payments into a more focused commerce solutions platform.

Adjusted operating income of $1.1 billion increased 22.1% year over year in the quarter under review. Adjusted operating margin expanded 110 basis points (bps) year over year on a normalized basis to 39.9%.

Total operating expenses of $3 billion increased 106.1% year over year in the first quarter. The increase was due to higher selling, general and administrative expenses, and cost of service. Interest and other expenses rose 63.2% year over year to $242.4 million.

GPN’s Financial Position (As of March 31, 2026)

Global Payments exited the first quarter with cash and cash equivalents of $5.9 billion, which decreased from $8.3 billion at 2025-end. Total assets of $64.3 billion rose from $53.3 billion at 2025-end.

Long-term debt amounted to $21 billion compared with $19.5 billion at 2025-end. The current portion of long-term debt totaled $1.6 billion at the first-quarter end.

Total equity of $24.5 billion rose from the figure of $23.6 billion at 2025-end.

GPN’s operating activities used $288.8 million of cash in the first quarter of 2026, down from $555.1 million generated a year ago.

Capital Deployment Update

The company entered into a $500 million accelerated share repurchase program. GPN repurchased shares worth $549.9 million in the first quarter of 2026.

The company declared a quarterly dividend of 25 cents per share, which will be paid out on June 26, 2026, to its shareholders of record as of June 12.

GPN Reaffirms 2026 Outlook

Adjusted net revenue growth on a constant currency basis, excluding dispositions, is still expected to be around 5% in 2026.

Adjusted EPS growth is still anticipated to be between 13% and 15% in 2026. GPN expects to convert almost 90% of adjusted net income into adjusted free cash flow.

Story Continues

The annual adjusted operating margin is expected to increase around 150 bps in 2026.

GPN’s Zacks Rank

GPN currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here.

How Did Peers Perform?

Several companies in the business services space, including Mastercard Incorporated MA, Visa Inc. V and Marsh & McLennan Companies, Inc. MRSH, have also reported their financial results for the March quarter of 2026. Here’s how they had performed:

Mastercard reported first-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings of $4.60 per share, which topped the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 4.6%. The bottom line improved 23.3% year over year. Net revenues advanced 15.8% year over year to $8.4 billion. MA’s quarterly results benefited from growing cross-border volumes and solid growth in value-added services revenues. However, the upside was partly offset by elevated operating expenses and higher payment network rebates from new and renewed deals.

Visa delivered second-quarter fiscal 2026 adjusted earnings of $3.31 per share, up 20% year over year and beat the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 7.1%. Net revenues came in at $11.23 billion, rising 17% year over year. V’s quarterly results reflected resilient spending trends, higher cross-border volumes and solid network activity, including a 9% year-over-year increase in payments volume on a constant-dollar basis. However, the upside was partly offset by increased operating expenses.

Marsh reported first-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings per share of $3.29, which surpassed the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 2.5%. The bottom line advanced 8% year over year. Consolidated revenues of $7.6 billion improved 8% year over year. The strong quarterly results benefited from solid growth in the Risk and Insurance Services and Consulting unit, particularly from the Marsh Risk, Guy Carpenter, Mercer and Marsh Management Consulting businesses. The upside was partially offset by elevated operating expenses, primarily due to increased compensation and benefits.

title: HES FinTech Expands Partnership with Acquired.com to Deliver Next-Generation Recurring Payments via Visa A2A
content:
VILNIUS, Lithuania, May 06, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--HES FinTech, a global provider of lending and debt collection software, has expanded its partnership with Acquired.com, a payments infrastructure provider specializing in recurring commerce. The latest development brings Commercial Variable Recurring Payments (cVRPs) powered by Visa A2A to HES LoanBox through a native, out-of-the-box integration.

Recurring payments are critical across lending, insurance, utilities, and collections, yet traditional methods like direct debit and card-on-file often trade off speed, cost, and reliability. Acquired.com solves this by unifying cards, Direct Debit, Open Banking, and cVRPs within a single infrastructure — now extended through its UK partnership with Visa.

cVRPs — the next evolution of recurring payment technology — enable real-time, bank-to-bank transactions through a structured consent model. Customers authorize once in their banking app, defining payment limits, frequency, and duration for full transparency and control.

Visa A2A delivers cVRPs via Faster Payments, with pre-transaction Confirmation of Funds checks that cut failures and boost operational efficiency.

At the core of the partnership is Acquired.com's API-first architecture, which embeds payment capabilities into HES LoanBox with rapid deployment and minimal engineering effort.

HES LoanBox clients — fintechs, banks, and financial institutions — gain immediate access to A2A payments within their workflows, reducing failed payments, improving cash flow visibility, and supporting multiple rails as market standards evolve. Borrowers, in turn, benefit from a streamlined repayment experience with clear consent, defined limits, and greater control over timing — reducing friction and building trust.

"Working with a provider that is deeply embedded in the UK fintech ecosystem allows us to deliver more relevant, compliant, and forward-looking payment capabilities to our clients."

Ivan Kovalenko, Founder & CEO, HES FinTech

"Our ongoing collaboration with HES FinTech enables us to embed advanced A2A capabilities directly into the platform, ensuring that users can manage collections and recurring payments with minimal friction. BCombining our payment infrastructure with LoanBox's automation streamlines operations and improves customer experience."

Gregory Cox, Founder & CEO, Acquired.com

About HES FinTech

Founded in 2012 in Vilnius, Lithuania, HES FinTech provides automated end-to-end lending and loan management software for banks and financial institutions worldwide, covering the full credit lifecycle — from origination and scoring to servicing and recovery.

Story Continues

About Acquired.com

Founded in 2016, Acquired.com delivers a unified payments infrastructure, helping businesses optimize recurring payments across multiple rails to reduce complexity and improve performance.

title: Kaspi.kz: The Market's Biggest Mispriced Monopoly--or a Hidden Fragility?
content:
This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

At first glance, Kaspi.kz (NASDAQ:KSPI) looks like the perfect emerging market compounder. A dominant super app. Explosive growth. High margins. Network effects that seem unbreakable. The kind of business investors dream about finding before the rest of the world catches on. But the deeper you go, the more complicated the story becomes. This is not just a fintech. It is not just an e-commerce platform. It is not even just a bank. Kaspi.kz is the digital infrastructure of an entire economy. And that distinction is precisely what makes it both incredibly powerful and potentially fragile.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 4 Warning Signs with KSPI. Is KSPI fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

This is a business that has effectively turned itself into the toll road of Kazakhstan's economic activity, monetizing payments, commerce, and credit in a tightly integrated loop. But when a company becomes this central, the upside compounds quicklyand so do the risks. The question is no longer whether Kaspi is a great business. The real question is whether you are underwriting a decade-long compounder or walking into a structurally misunderstood risk.

At roughly 6 earnings, the market is not pricing Kaspi as a normal compounder. It is pricing a scenario where the expansion initiatives, especially Turkey, do not merely disappoint, but actively destroy value. That is the real setup. If the core Kazakhstan platform remains intact and management does not keep pouring capital into weak international expansion, the current multiple looks too low. If Turkey works, the upside is obvious. If Turkey fails and consumes capital, the downside is real. The investment question is not whether Kaspi is a great business. It is whether the market has become too pessimistic about what happens next.

This Is Not a Super App. This Is a Closed Economic System

To understand Kaspi, you have to strip away the labels. Calling it a super app undersells what it actually is. Kaspi operates a closed-loop economic system that connects consumers, merchants, payments, lending, and government services inside one digital environment. That combination is not just rare. It is the reason the company earns platform-like economics in a market where traditional financial institutions still carry bank-like complexity.

The business is built on three core engines that reinforce each other. The payments platform drives daily engagement through peer-to-peer transfers, bill payments, and QR transactions. The marketplace monetizes that engagement by connecting millions of consumers to hundreds of thousands of merchants, extracting take rates on gross merchandise value. The fintech layer sits on top, providing high-yield lending products such as buy-now-pay-later and consumer loans, funded by local deposits and powered by proprietary data.

Story Continues

Kaspi.kz: The Market's Biggest Mispriced Monopoly--or a Hidden Fragility?

The scale is staggering. In 2025, Kaspi generated over KZT 4 trillion in revenue, up from roughly KZT 2.5 trillion the year prior, representing structural growth rather than cyclical expansion. Total payment volume exceeded KZT 12 trillion in a single quarter, while marketplace GMV reached approximately KZT 6.7 trillion annually. The fintech segment alone produced KZT 420 billion in quarterly revenue, supported by a total finance value of over KZT 3 trillion. These are not startup numbers. This is an economy being monetized in real time.

What makes the model extraordinary is not just the size, but the efficiency. Customer acquisition cost is effectively negligible, estimated at under $2 per user, because the platform acquires users organically through utility. Consumers do not download Kaspi to shop. They download it to live. They pay taxes, register vehicles, transfer money, and access government services through the app. Commerce and lending are layered on top of that behavior. This is not a funnel. It is an ecosystem.

The Moat Is RealAnd It Is Getting Stronger

Most companies claim network effects. Kaspi actually has them. And not just the standard two-sided marketplace dynamic. This is a multi-layered reinforcement system where each component strengthens the others in ways that are difficult to replicate.

On the consumer side, Kaspi has reached near-total penetration in Kazakhstan, with over 14 million monthly active users in a country of roughly 19 million people. Engagement is equally impressive, with users averaging more than 70 transactions per month. This is not occasional usage. This is daily dependency.

On the merchant side, the platform has become indispensable. Kaspi Pay processes approximately 80% of e-commerce payments in the country and over 70% of all non-cash retail transactions. For a merchant, opting out of Kaspi is not a strategic decision. It is economic suicide. This level of dependency creates pricing power that is both subtle and powerful. The company has steadily increased its marketplace take rate from around 10.1% to 10.9%, not through aggressive fee hikes, but by layering high-margin services such as advertising and logistics onto the platform.

Importantly, this moat is not just economic. It is behavioral and institutional. The integration of government services creates a level of stickiness that goes beyond convenience. Leaving Kaspi is not just inconvenient. It disrupts your daily life. That kind of lock-in is extremely rare outside of a handful of ecosystems like Tencent in China.

Growth Is No Longer the Question. Capital Discipline Is

The domestic story is largely proven. Kazakhstan has already moved from cash-heavy commerce to a highly digitized economy, and Kaspi was one of the main architects of that transition. The core platform has scale, engagement, merchant dependency, and daily utility. The question is no longer whether Kaspi works in Kazakhstan. It clearly does. The question is whether management can expand beyond Kazakhstan without damaging the economics that made the core business so valuable.

That is why Turkey matters. The Hepsiburada acquisition gives Kaspi access to a much larger market, with more than 85 million people and far lower e-commerce engagement than Kazakhstan. On paper, the opportunity is obvious. If Kaspi can lift transaction frequency, improve monetization, and layer payments or fintech into the Turkish ecosystem, the upside is meaningful. Turkey becomes an option on turning a domestic monopoly into a regional platform.

But the risk is equally clear. Exporting a super app is not the same as building one. Kazakhstan offered a rare combination of underbanked consumers, fragmented retail, and deep government integration. Turkey is larger, more competitive, more inflationary, and more operationally complex. The issue is not simply whether Turkey works. The issue is whether management keeps allocating incremental capital if it does not.

That distinction matters. If Turkey struggles but does not require heavy additional capital, the downside is contained and the core Kazakhstan business remains intact. If Turkey works, Kaspi gets earnings growth and a stronger regional narrative. But if Turkey becomes an open-ended capital sink, then the market's current discount is justified. At roughly 6 earnings, investors are not being asked to pay much for Turkey. They are being asked to decide whether Turkey destroys the value of the core.

The Financial Engine Is Still Exceptional

Despite the growing complexity, the core financial engine remains extremely strong. Kaspi continues to generate high returns on capital, driven by a combination of near-zero customer acquisition costs, high engagement, and deeply integrated infrastructure. The payments layer provides the volume and data, the marketplace monetizes that activity through take rates and services, and the fintech segment captures the highest returns, with portfolio yields approaching the high teens and relatively low default rates supported by proprietary underwriting.

What makes this system powerful is how efficiently it scales. As transaction volumes increase, fixed costs are spread across a larger base, creating operating leverage that drives incremental margin expansion. At the same time, Kaspi's ability to route transactions through its own infrastructure, bypassing traditional networks like Visa (NYSE:V) and Mastercard (NYSE:MA), structurally improves unit economics. This is not just a digital business. It is a vertically integrated financial and commercial system that captures value at multiple layers of the transaction flow.

The Risks Are RealBut Do They Break the Core?

This is where the narrative breaks. Kaspi is a high-quality system built on top of emerging market risk, and that distinction matters. The risks are not theoretical. But the investment question is more specific: do they permanently impair the core Kazakhstan platform, or do they merely cap the multiple?

Regulation is the first pressure point. Kazakhstan's updated tax framework pushes the corporate rate toward 25% for financial institutions, and any combination of higher taxes, lending caps, or tighter oversight would hit the most profitable layer of the business. Kaspi's fintech segment benefits from high-teens yields and strong incremental margins. If those economics reset lower, earnings power falls. But unless regulation damages engagement, payments volume, merchant dependency, or credit quality, the core platform remains intact.

Governance and geopolitical exposure create the second discount. Insider ownership sits close to 70%, which aligns management economically but limits minority influence. The Culper Research attack in 2024 made the issue visible. The short case did not mainly challenge Kaspi's consumer engagement or marketplace take rates. It targeted geopolitical exposure, sanctions risk, and non-resident account growth after the Russia-Ukraine conflict. Management pushed back with data showing the business remains overwhelmingly domestic, but the episode created reputational damage, legal uncertainty, and a credibility discount that may continue to cap the multiple.

Accounting quality is the third concern. Kaspi has disclosed material weaknesses in internal controls around Expected Credit Loss models, which matters because fintech lending is central to reported profitability. For a company built on large-scale algorithmic lending, impairment assumptions are not a footnote. They are part of the earnings engine. External claims of unauthorized or off-book loans add another layer of uncertainty. Even if these claims are overstated, they raise the question that matters most for valuation: how much confidence should investors place in the reported earnings base?

Finally, execution risk is now concentrated in Turkey. This is not an extension of the Kazakhstan model. It is a test of management's capital discipline. If Turkey proves capable of becoming self-funding, or if management limits incremental capital deployment, it becomes closer to an option than an open-ended capital sink. If management continues to allocate capital into a lower-return market, it becomes a drag on the entire investment case. That is why the stock trades where it does. Complexity has risen, and when complexity rises, multiples rarely stay the same.

Valuation A Great Business Priced for a Bad Outcome

At around $7475 per share, Kaspi trades at roughly 67 trailing earnings and about 6 forward earnings. That is not a premium compounder multiple. It is a stress multiple. The market is not saying Kaspi is a bad business. It is saying the durability of its earnings is uncertain.

Start with the earnings base. Kaspi generated roughly KZT 4.0 trillion in revenue and approximately KZT 1.21.3 trillion in annualized net income, supported by a dominant Kazakhstan platform across payments, marketplace, and fintech. On the surface, that is the profile of a high-return platform. But at 6 earnings, the market is effectively assuming that some combination of regulation, lower returns on capital, Turkey dilution, and governance discount will pressure future earnings and prevent a premium multiple.

A simple sum-of-the-parts framing helps clarify the bet. The core Kazakhstan platform is the crown jewel: dominant, high-return, deeply embedded, and cash generative. That business alone arguably deserves more than a stressed 6 multiple if investors believed the earnings were durable. The international segment, mainly Turkey, is the swing factor. It is either an option on future growth or a drag on returns. At the current price, the market appears to assign little value to that option and is instead treating it as a potential source of value destruction.

That creates three clean outcomes. If expansion is curtailed, or if Turkey underperforms without requiring meaningful additional capital, the core Kazakhstan platform remains intact. In that scenario, the business does not need heroic growth to re-rate. A move from roughly 6 earnings to even 1012 on approximately KZT 1.2 trillion of earnings would imply substantial upside. If expansion works, the upside is stronger: higher EPS, a larger addressable market, and a credible path from domestic monopoly to regional platform. But if expansion destroys value through continued investment into lower-return markets, the current multiple is not a bargain. It is the market correctly discounting future capital misallocation.

That is the real valuation question. Kaspi looks cheap only if you believe the core system remains stable and management stays disciplined. The low multiple is not a mistake. It is the market pricing regulation, capital allocation risk, and governance uncertainty all at once. If those risks do not materialize, the stock is clearly undervalued relative to the quality of the business. If even part of that risk stack plays out, the current valuation may be accurate. This is not a valuation problem. It is a trust problem.

So What Are You Really Buying?

At its core, Kaspi.kz remains one of the most extraordinary platform businesses to emerge from an emerging market. It has built a digital ecosystem that captures the flow of money across an entire economy, with network effects, pricing power, and engagement metrics that rival some of the best platforms globally.

But the investment case no longer rests on proving that Kaspi is a great business. That has already been established. The real question is whether the market is too pessimistic about what happens next. If the core Kazakhstan platform remains intact and management avoids turning international expansion into an open-ended capital sink, the current valuation looks too low. If Turkey works, the upside becomes even more interesting. But if expansion destroys value, the discount is justified.

The market is not mispricing Kaspi's quality. It is pricing a specific outcome: that expansion will dilute returns, governance risk will cap the multiple, and the core platform will not deserve a premium valuation. The opportunity is not in discovering Kaspi's quality. The opportunity is in deciding whether the market has become too pessimistic about its durability.

title: Visa's Q2 Beat Sparks Estimate Upgrades: Should Investors Jump In Now?
content:
Wall Street sentiment on Visa Inc. V is improving after a strong second-quarter fiscal 2026 performance, and estimate revisions are now backing that optimism. Over the past week, the Zacks Consensus Estimate for fiscal 2026 and 2027 EPS saw nine upward revisions each, a strong signal that analysts are growing more confident in Visa’s earnings path.Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

For fiscal 2026, Visa’s EPS is now projected at $13.01, implying 13.4% year-over-year growth. For fiscal 2027, the estimate has moved up to $14.74, pointing to another 13.3% increase. Revenue expectations are moving higher, too. Analysts now forecast $44.96 billion in fiscal 2026 revenue and $49.66 billion in fiscal 2027, indicating growth of 12.4% and 10.5%, respectively.

Visa’s consistency adds weight to the optimism. The company has beaten EPS estimates in each of the past four quarters, with an average surprise of 3.2%.

Visa Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS SurpriseVisa Inc. Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Visa Inc. price-consensus-eps-surprise-chart | Visa Inc. Quote

So, what’s driving this confidence? The answer sits in Visa’s Q2 results.

Q2 Was a Clean, High-Quality Beat

Visa posted adjusted earnings of $3.31 per share, up 20% year over year and ahead of the Zacks Consensus Estimate by 7.1%. Net revenues climbed 17% to $11.23 billion, beating expectations by 5.1%.

The underlying transaction engine stayed strong. On a constant-dollar basis, cross-border volume rose 12%, reflecting steady international travel demand and continued strength in global e-commerce. Payment volumes grew 9%, while total processed transactions hit 66.1 billion, up 9% year over year.

Visa’s model is built for scale and stability. Whether consumers are spending on travel, dining, groceries, retail or subscriptions, Visa earns its share simply by keeping the payments flowing. That’s why its results tend to hold up even when consumer behavior shifts.

For more insights, read our blog: Visa Q2 Earnings Beat Estimates on Payment Volume Strength.

VAS Becoming a Bigger Piece of the Story

Value-Added Services (VAS) revenues surged 27% in constant dollars to $3.3 billion, and now make up roughly 30% of Visa’s total net revenues. Growth was fueled by expanding demand for network products and marketing services, both of which carry attractive economics and deepen Visa’s client relationships. With major global sporting events like the FIFA World Cup and the Olympic Games approaching,marketing and analytics demand could stay elevated, helping diversify revenues and lift margin quality.

Visa’s Stablecoin Strategy Is Starting to Scale

Visa’s progress in stablecoins and blockchain infrastructure continues to stand out. While management has been careful not to overhype stablecoins as an everyday consumer payment tool, the numbers suggest real momentum in practical use cases. During fiscal Q2, stablecoin-linked card payment volumes jumped nearly 200% year over year, supported by more than 160 programs worldwide.

Story Continues

Its stablecoin settlement business has reached a $7 billion annual run rate, up more than 50% sequentially. In April 2026, Visa expanded its global stablecoin settlement pilot to support nine blockchains, widening its reach and strengthening its role as a key connector between digital assets and traditional payment rails.

Visa also acknowledged that stablecoins still lack strong everyday use cases in developed markets like the United States, the U.K. and Europe.Digital payments are already fast, smooth and widely accepted, leaving limited urgency for consumers to switch. But cross-border payments remain a different story. Stablecoins can reduce friction, shorten settlement times, lower costs, and improve liquidity, benefits that matter for financial institutions and global enterprises.

Buybacks and Dividends Continue at Full Speed

Visa continues to pair growth with capital returns. During the quarter, the company returned $9.2 billion to shareholders, including $7.9 billion in buybacks and $1.3 billion in dividends. It authorized a new $20 billion multi-year share repurchase program in April. Visa’s dividend yield sits at 0.83%, higher than Mastercard Incorporated’s MA 0.70%, though still below American Express Company AXP at 1.20%.

The Stock Has Held Up, But It’s Not Cheap

Visa shares have gained 6.4% over the past month, slightly ahead of the industry’s 6% rise, though still behind the S&P 500’s 9.9% gain. Mastercard slipped 0.3%, while American Express rose 2.9% over the same period.

1-Month Price Performance: V, MA, AXP, Industry & S&P 500Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Valuation remains elevated, but that’s not new for Visa. The stock is trading at 23.00X forward earnings, well above the industry average of 16.81X, but still below Visa’s five-year median of 26.03X. For comparison, Mastercard trades at 24.16X, while American Express trades at 17.12X. Investors are still paying a premium for Visa’s stability and global dominance.Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Key Risks to Monitor

Still, Visa’s outlook isn’t risk-free.Stablecoins could eventually become a disruptive force if major retailers or technology companies launch their own payment ecosystems at scale. If that happens, some transaction volume could bypass traditional card rails, creating long-term pressure on interchange-driven economics.

Visa is also being challenged from two sides. Fintech companies are trying to redesign payment economics from the ground up, while real-time payment networks and upgraded legacy systems are narrowing the gap in speed and efficiency. The more viable alternatives exist, the harder it becomes for Visa to defend premium pricing.

Regulatory scrutiny is another major overhang. In the United States, the Department of Justice has accused Visa and Mastercard of using market dominance to maintain elevated merchant fees. The proposed Credit Card Competition Act could also reshape routing rules, potentially changing how payment networks capture value.

Europe remains sensitive too. In June 2025, the Competition Appeal Tribunal in London ruled that Visa and Mastercard’s multi-lateral interchange fees breached European competition law. The U.K. Payment Systems Regulator is expected to introduce fee caps, which could limit growth in the region. Meanwhile, several U.K. banks are exploring domestic alternatives, which could gradually reduce dependence on U.S.-based card networks.

Conclusion

Visa continues to deliver steady execution, backed by strong payment volume trends, resilient cross-border activity, and accelerating value-added services growth. Its fiscal Q2 results and rising earnings estimates suggest the business remains on a solid track, while stablecoin-linked card volumes and settlement expansion highlight longer-term upside optionality.

However, the stock’s premium valuation limits near-term upside, and rising regulatory scrutiny in the U.S. and Europe remains an overhang. Competition from fintechs and real-time payment networks also adds pressure over time. Given this balance, Visa carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). title: Is It Time To Reassess Visa (V) After Recent Regulatory Fee Scrutiny?
content:
Make better investment decisions with Simply Wall St's easy, visual tools that give you a competitive edge.

If you are wondering whether Visa at around US$322 per share offers good value or whether you are paying up for quality, this breakdown will help you frame that question clearly. The stock has recently moved 4.1% over the past week and 7.1% over the past month, while the year to date return of 7.1% decline and 1 year return of 6.7% decline contrast with a 3 year return of 41.2% and 5 year return of 48.2%. Recent headlines on Visa have focused on its role in global payments, regulatory attention on fees, and ongoing partnerships with financial institutions. All of these factors influence how investors think about growth and risk, and they provide useful context when you compare them with the stock's recent price moves. Visa currently has a valuation score of 2 out of 6. Next you will see how different valuation methods assess the stock, followed by a framework that can help you think about value even more clearly.

Visa scores just 2/6 on our valuation checks. See what other red flags we found in the full valuation breakdown.

Approach 1: Visa Excess Returns Analysis

The Excess Returns model looks at how efficiently a company turns its equity base into earnings, after accounting for the return that shareholders require. Instead of focusing on cash flows, it compares the return on equity with the cost of equity to estimate what each dollar of book value is worth.

For Visa, book value is US$18.64 per share and stable earnings per share are estimated at US$14.80, based on weighted future Return on Equity estimates from 9 analysts. The cost of equity is put at US$1.57 per share, which implies an excess return of US$13.23 per share. That is consistent with an average Return on Equity of 68.84% and a stable book value estimate of US$21.49 per share from the same analyst set.

Using these inputs in the Excess Returns model results in an intrinsic value estimate of about US$375.09 per share. Compared with a current share price around US$322, this corresponds to roughly a 14.1% discount, suggesting Visa stock appears undervalued on this approach.

Approach 2: Visa Price vs Earnings

For a profitable company like Visa, the P/E ratio is a useful gauge because it links what you pay for each share with the earnings that support that price. Investors usually accept a higher P/E when they expect stronger earnings growth or see lower risk, and look for a lower P/E when growth expectations are modest or risks are higher.
